analysis.one_liner: Pauses new plastics-plant permits, tightens pollution rules at petrochemical facilities, and cuts single-use plastics.
analysis.headline: Introduced with seven Senate sponsors in April 2024, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Environmental Protection Agency to stop issuing new permits for plastics and petrochemical facilities until stricter air and water pollution rules were written. It would have forced existing plants to install continuous emissions monitoring, meet tougher discharge limits, prove they can pay for cleanup, and barred new plants within 5 miles of schools, homes, or parks. It also would have required producers to cut single-use plastic packaging and scale up reusable and refillable systems, with grants favoring low-income communities and communities of color near these facilities.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near plastics and petrochemical plants — disproportionately low-income communities and communities of color — would get pollution monitoring, a say in permits, and community benefit agreements. Consumers would see fewer single-use plastics and more refillable options, and taxpayers would avoid cleanup costs plants currently leave behind.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a pause on new federal and state permits for covered plastics and petrochemical facilities — and bans export of covered plastic products — until EPA finalizes stricter air and water rules under the bill [S2].

Requires EPA to write new Clean Air standards for petrochemical and polymer plants, restrict flaring to safety-only cases, and mandate continuous emissions monitoring with real-time public reporting of the data [S2].

Requires covered facilities to run an environmental justice assessment on every permit, hold hearings in fenceline communities with translation services, negotiate community benefit agreements, and run perimeter air monitoring and water testing [S2].

Sets federal targets to cut single-use plastic packaging and food-service products by at least 25% by 2034 and reach at least 30% reuse and refill by 2034, with grants to build refill infrastructure [S2].
Bars new or expanded plastics facilities within 5 miles of a school, residence, daycare, nursing home, hospital, clinic, place of worship, park, playground, or community center [S2].
Requires financial assurance so plant owners demonstrate enough money to safely close facilities or respond to an accidental release, rather than leaving those costs to the public [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Plastics and petrochemical producers bear new compliance costs — stricter air and water standards, monitoring, financial assurance, and a permit moratorium. Beverage, packaged food, and consumer goods companies would have to redesign packaging and build reuse systems, and some of those costs would likely reach consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The permit moratorium applies to all covered facilities — not just the worst polluters — so even projects with strong controls could be delayed until every required rule under the bill is in effect, potentially holding back investment in plants that would replace older, dirtier ones [S2].

Compliance costs for stricter emissions limits, monitoring, and packaging redesign would be borne first by producers and would likely be passed partly to consumers in the prices of goods and food service [S2].
A flat 5-mile siting ban around any community building or area is rigid and could block facility construction or expansion in regions where plants anchor local jobs [S2].

The bill excludes pyrolysis and gasification from the National Recycling Strategy and directs EPA to list discarded PVC as hazardous waste, which waste-industry groups argue removes disposal options and raises waste-handling costs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people living next to these plants, the health protections — monitoring, cumulative-impact reviews, community benefit agreements, and financial assurance — outweigh the compliance costs, which are borne industry-wide. The main honest concern is design: the bill pauses all new covered facilities rather than targeting the worst, and its siting ban is blunt. Consumers would pay some of the tab through prices, but the bill's targets are phased over a decade.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025 [S4][S1].

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Protecting Communities from Plastics Act of 2024 on April 18, 2024, joined by six other senators: Merkley, Van Hollen, Sanders, Durbin, Welch, and Markey [S1][S2].
The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on April 18, 2024; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill was not reintroduced or acted on further, so it never received a floor or committee vote [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastics and petrochemical producers are better off — no permit moratorium, no stricter air and water standards, and no single-use plastic reduction targets took effect. Fenceline communities got none of the promised monitoring or protections.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and all six cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-led committee never advanced it [S2][S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would impose a permit moratorium, stricter Clean Air and Clean Water standards, continuous monitoring, financial assurance, and a hazardous-waste listing for discarded PVC — costs the industry bears to reduce pollution that today lands mainly on neighboring communities.

The bill bans export of covered petrochemical products during the pause period and is premised on cutting petrochemicals' growing share of oil and gas demand, trimming a growth market for fossil fuel producers.

industries.industry: Beverage, packaged food, and consumer goods companies
industries.note: Producers would face at least 25% single-use packaging reduction and 30% reuse and refill targets by 2034, forcing packaging redesign; some costs would pass to consumers, while refill infrastructure grants could offset part of the transition.

The bill counts pyrolysis, gasification, and incineration facilities as covered facilities subject to the permit moratorium and bars EPA from folding them into the National Recycling Strategy, cutting off a disposal pathway the industry markets as recycling.

industries.industry: Reusable packaging and refill service providers
industries.note: The bill funds a grant program for refill and reuse projects, installs water refill stations, and mandates reuse targets, creating demand for refill systems and sanitation infrastructure.
